adds.title: Penitenciarias Nacionales de Honduras: una tortura para personas LGTBI - Corresponsales Clave
adds.summary: Corresponsales Clave (trans activist Kendra Jordany, 6 Sep 2017), drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT: trans women in Honduras' national penitentiaries are held in the MEN'S system. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module (located beside the mentally-ill unit); trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women ('la policia... dicen que ellas son hombres'); conjugal visits are denied. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her feminine belongings returned. Documents birth-sex placement with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy.

adds.title: HRW, 'Every Day I Live in Fear': Violence and Discrimination Against LGBT People in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, and Obstacles to Asylum in the United States
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch (7 Oct 2020), Honduras section: 'Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse.' A Honduran judge told HRW of a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards; the judge said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate: 'There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.' Independent confirmation that placement operates by birth sex in the men's system, with documented sexual violence and official inaction (as of 2020).

records.note: Placement practice documented for Honduras: with no legal gender recognition, trans women are housed by birth sex in men's facilities. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara they are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module inside the men's prison, forced to cut their hair and present as male (Corresponsales Clave, Sep 2017); a Marcala case saw a trans woman's clothes seized and hair cut until CPTRT intervention had her isolated from the men. HRW (Oct 2020) states plainly that Honduras 'places transgender women in men's prisons' and documents a judge-reported rape case with guard complicity and no investigation; a 2023 statement by trans-rights association Cozumel Trans (HCH) further documents abusive conditions in Centros Penitenciarios. No statute, court ruling, or formal policy requiring placement by gender identity was found; no dedicated trans custody unit exists beyond the de facto LGBTI grouping, and protective segregation has been applied ad hoc after NGO intervention.

adds.title: Jennifer, la mujer trans que sobrevivio a las torturas en las carceles del regimen de excepcion (GatoEncerrado)
adds.summary: GatoEncerrado (Oscar Hernandez, 26 Feb 2024): since the state of exception began (Mar 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. Jennifer, arrested 14 Apr 2022 in San Salvador, was held first at the 'El Penalito' police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair ('para que sepan lo que son'), singled her out with another trans woman (Rosa) for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after ~4 months finding the arrest unsupported, while Rosa remains imprisoned. Organisations (Socorro Juridico Humanista, Cristosal) link the abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law. Documents birth-sex placement in the general prison system with trans-targeted abuse and no special custody provision.

records.note: No statute, court ruling, or policy on trans-prisoner placement was found for El Salvador; there is no Gender Identity Law, and the documented practice under the state of exception (2022- ) is birth-sex placement in the general system: Jennifer's case (Apr 2022) shows forced head-shaving, trans-targeted cell punishments and denial of HIV care inside ordinary prisons, with orgs (Socorro Juridico Humanista, Cristosal) confirming the lack of any protection mechanism (GatoEncerrado, Feb 2024). A second candidate (La Prensa Grafica, Sep 2024, on gender violence inside prisons) was not retrievable (empty 202 response) and could not be verified; no trans-specific solitary/administrative-segregation practice or special custody unit is documented.

adds.title: Transexuales reclusos en carceles nacionales podran optar entre prision de hombres o mujeres (AmeliaRueda.com)
adds.summary: AmeliaRueda.com (Alonso Mata Blanco, 25 Jun 2017): Costa Rica's Justice Ministry (Vice-Minister Marco Feoli) announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility - relocation to the facility matching gender identity, strictly voluntary, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners, an exclusive module for trans people was under consideration, and Spain's system was cited as the model (protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016). Official policy-level documentation of placement-by-gender-identity in the regional context.

adds.title: Stephanie, la transgenero que vive en la carcel rodeada de hombres | CR Hoy
adds.summary: CRHoy (Javier Paniagua, 22 Jun 2019): Stephanie, a trans woman serving ~6 years for drug-trafficking complicity, is held at CAI Orosi de Cartago - a men's facility ('en esa sede solo hay hombres'); she transitioned while incarcerated and says prison offers 'solo hay dos opciones: o sos hombre o mujer aqui'. The Justice Ministry told CRHoy there were 23 transgender people in the national system at the time. Stephanie recounts identity-targeted abuse including a broomstick-handle rape at La Reforma (Alajuela) witnessed by a custodian. Shows that despite the 2017 choice policy, trans women were still found in men's facilities in 2019 and faced violence with custodial inaction.

records.note: Costa Rica is the one Central American jurisdiction with an explicit placement mechanism: since June 2017 the Justice Ministry allows self-identified trans prisoners to choose a men's or women's facility (voluntary, with psychological/social-work assessment, a trans-inmate census, and a possible dedicated module - AmeliaRueda, 2017). Enforcement is uneven in practice: in 2019 the ministry counted 23 transgender people in the system and trans women were still held in men's centres (Stephanie at CAI Orosi; broomstick rape at La Reforma witnessed by a custodian - CRHoy, 2019). No court ruling on placement and no trans-specific solitary/administrative-segregation practice was located.

no prison-housing data found: after 2 web-search rounds and 2 candidate fetches (a Panama civil-society LGBTIQ UPR submission, OHCHR UPR docs; and WOLA's regional study 'Mujeres trans privadas de libertad' - the latter mentions Panama only in its legal-identity-change table, without prison-housing content), no Panama-specific policy, documented case, court ruling, special custody unit, or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners was located. Panama has no legal gender recognition (per the record's existing sources), so formal classification is binary by birth sex, but no fetched source documents how trans prisoners are actually housed; the MINGOB open-data prison census and DGSP portal surfaced in search offer only binary sex breakdowns.
